primer.title: Who owns it, who is looking at it
body: Every value has exactly one owner. Passing a non-`Copy` value **by value** moves it: the old name stays in scope but may not be read again.
Borrows come in two kinds: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T` — never both at once.
A borrow lasts until its *last use*, not until the end of the block:

```
let first = inv.first();   // shared borrow starts
inv.add("torch");          // needs &mut: conflict
println!("{:?}", first);   // ...because it is used here
```
When reading for these errors: find each call that takes `T` or `&mut T`, then look *below* it for another use of the same name.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line the compiler rejects.
exercises.rationale: Line 11 reads `vec0` after line 9 moved it into `fill_vec` (E0382). `Vec` is not `Copy`, so passing it by value gives it away.

lineRationales.9: This is where `vec0` is moved — and moving is legal. The error is reported where the moved value is used again.
lineRationales.2: Rebinding a parameter as `mut` is fine: the function owns `vec`, so it may decide to mutate it.
lineRationales.12: `vec1` owns the vector that `fill_vec` returned. Nothing has moved out of it.

exercises.fallbackRationale: That line compiles. Look for a value that is used after it was passed by value.

exercises.prompt: This does not compile. What does the compiler object to?

options.text: E0596: `vec` is not declared mutable, so it cannot be borrowed as mutable on line 2
options.rationale: `push` takes `&mut self`. Owning a value is not enough: the binding itself must be `mut` (`mut vec: Vec<i32>`).

options.text: E0382: `vec0` is used after being moved on line 8
options.rationale: `vec0` is moved on line 8 but never touched again. `vec1` is a different value.

options.text: E0308: `fill_vec` returns `()` because line 2 ends in `;`
options.rationale: The function's last expression is `vec` on line 3, without a semicolon.

options.text: E0507: `vec` cannot be moved out of the function
options.rationale: Returning an owned value is the normal way to hand ownership back.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line the compiler rejects.
exercises.rationale: Line 5 takes a second `&mut x` while `y` is still alive — `y` is used again on line 7 (E0499).

lineRationales.4: The first mutable borrow is fine. It becomes a problem only because it is still in use when line 5 asks for another one.
lineRationales.7: This use is what keeps `y` alive across line 5 — but the compiler reports the error at the second borrow, not here.
lineRationales.10: By line 10 both `y` and `z` have had their last use, so reading `x` is allowed again.

exercises.fallbackRationale: That line compiles. Count the `&mut` borrows of `x` that are alive at the same time.

exercises.prompt: Same lines as before, reordered. What happens now?

options.rationale: A borrow ends at its last use. `y` is finished after line 5, so line 7 may borrow `x` mutably again.

options.text: It does not compile: E0499, `x` is mutably borrowed twice
options.rationale: Two `&mut` borrows conflict only if they are alive at the same time. `y` is never used after line 5.
`push` appends at the end, in program order.

options.text: It does not compile: `x` is still mutably borrowed on line 10
options.rationale: `z` has its last use on line 8, so the borrow is over before `x` is read.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line the compiler rejects.
exercises.rationale: Line 14 borrows `data` after line 13 moved it into `get_char`, whose parameter is `String`, not `&String` (E0382).

lineRationales.13: Passing `data` by value is legal — it is simply the last time `main` may use it. The error appears at the next use.
lineRationales.1: A function is free to take ownership. This signature is the *cause*, but not where the compiler reports the error.
lineRationales.5: Taking `&String` only borrows. This function is the well-behaved one.

exercises.fallbackRationale: That line compiles. Compare the two function signatures: which one takes ownership?

exercises.prompt: This does not compile. What does the compiler object to?
code: let mut inv = Inventory { items: vec![], capacity: 3 };

options.text: E0502: `inv` is borrowed mutably on line 26 while `first` still borrows it
options.rationale: `first` holds a shared borrow that lives until the `println!` on line 28. `add` needs `&mut self` in between.

options.text: E0382: `inv` was moved into `first` on line 25
E0499: `inv` is borrowed mutably twice (lines 23 and 26)
options.rationale: The mutable borrow on line 23 ends when that call returns. Sequential `&mut` borrows are fine.

options.text: E0308: `add` returns `bool` but the result is unused
options.rationale: Ignoring a `bool` is legal; only `#[must_use]` types warn.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line the compiler rejects.
code: fn archive(order: Order, store: &mut HashMap<u32, Order>) {
exercises.rationale: Line 26 reads `order` after line 24 moved it into `archive` (E0382). The move itself is legal; the later use is what fails.

lineRationales.24: This is where `order` is moved — and moving is allowed. The error is reported where the moved value is used again.
lineRationales.21: `clone()` makes an independent copy, so `order` is still owned by `main` afterwards.
lineRationales.10: `order.id` is a `u32`, which is `Copy`; it is read before `order` itself moves into the map.

exercises.fallbackRationale: That line compiles. Look for a value that is used after ownership has been given away.
